Understanding Confidence

Confidence is not a personality you are born with. In this module you learn what psychologists mean by self-efficacy, where it comes from, how to catch and question the unhelpful thoughts that hold you back, how old experiences shape today, and how to stay humble without shrinking.
What confidence is: self-efficacy and its four sources
Define confidence as belief in your ability to handle a specific task
Name the four sources of self-efficacy described by Albert Bandura
Rate your own confidence in three real situations on a 0 to 10 scale
Explain why confidence can grow with practice at any age

Many women think confidence means feeling no fear, talking loudly, or never doubting yourself. That is not what researchers mean. In psychology, the most useful idea is **self-efficacy**: your belief that you can carry out a particular task and manage what happens. The Canadian-American psychologist **Albert Bandura** introduced the idea in 1977, and it has been studied for decades in schools, workplaces and health programmes.

Notice two things in that definition. First, it is about **a task**, not your whole self. You can feel very sure of yourself cooking jollof rice for fifty guests and very unsure about speaking at a PTA meeting. Second, it is about **handling** the situation, not about a perfect result. A confident woman still expects some problems. She simply believes she can deal with them.
A woman standing tall with a calm, sure expression
Confidence is belief that you can handle a task, not the absence of fear.
Confidence and self-esteem are not the same

**Self-esteem** is how much you value yourself as a person overall. **Self-efficacy** is how able you feel in a specific area. They often move together, but not always. A woman can have good self-esteem ("I am a person of worth") and still have low self-efficacy for using a laptop. This course works mostly on self-efficacy, because it is practical: you can build it one task at a time, and every gain also feeds your self-esteem.

**Mastery experiences** are the most powerful because they are evidence you produced yourself. That is why this course keeps asking you to do small, real actions and keep proof of them. Words of encouragement help, but one completed task often does more than a hundred kind words.

**Vicarious experience** works best when the model is like you. Watching a celebrity can inspire, but watching your neighbour who started with the same capital is more convincing. **Physical states** matter because your body sends signals. Sweaty palms before an interview are normal. If you tell yourself, "My body is getting ready," you are more likely to keep going than if you tell yourself, "This proves I cannot do it."

Each small action adds evidence, and evidence is what grows self-efficacy.
Three myths that keep women stuck
**"Confident people are not afraid."** False. Many skilled speakers and leaders report nerves. Confidence is acting while some fear is present.
**"You are born with it or you are not."** Bandura's research shows self-efficacy changes with experience. It can grow at 25, 45 or 65.
**"I will start when I feel confident."** Usually the order is the opposite. Action comes first, and the feeling follows the evidence.
Worked example: rating confidence by task
For example, Ngozi is 38, sells foodstuff in a market in Enugu and wants to grow her business. She rates her confidence from 0 (not at all sure) to 10 (completely sure) for three tasks.
Weighing and pricing rice for customers: 9 out of 10. Source: she has done it daily for twelve years (mastery).
Sending a business price list on WhatsApp to 30 customers: 4 out of 10. She has rarely used WhatsApp Business.
Asking her cooperative for a loan of about ₦200,000 (approximate): 3 out of 10. She has never spoken at a meeting.
She picks the WhatsApp task first because it is the lowest risk, and asks her niece to show her once (vicarious) then does it herself (mastery).

After sending the list and getting five orders, Ngozi re-rates the WhatsApp task at 7. Her overall "I am not confident" story is replaced by a clearer picture: confident in some areas, still growing in others.
This course is not therapy

The tools here are self-help skills based on well-known psychology. If low mood, worry or fear is stopping you from sleeping, eating, working or caring for your family for more than two weeks, please talk to a doctor or a trained mental health professional. Asking for help is a strong step, not a weakness.

The inner critic: catching and reframing unhelpful thoughts
Recognise six common thinking traps
Separate a situation, a thought and a feeling
Complete a simple five-column thought record
Write a balanced replacement thought that you can believe

Most of us carry an inner voice that comments on everything we do. Sometimes it is helpful ("Check the change before the customer leaves"). Often it is harsh: "You will embarrass yourself", "Who do you think you are?", "You always get it wrong." This harsh voice is often called the **inner critic**. You cannot switch it off, but you can learn to question it instead of obeying it.

The method in this lesson comes from **cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)**, a well-researched approach developed by psychiatrist Aaron Beck. You do not need a therapist to use its basic self-help tools. The NHS in the UK teaches the same steps to the public as "catch it, check it, change it".
A woman sorting floating thought bubbles into order
Reframing means sorting your thoughts and keeping the ones that fit the facts.
Situation, thought, feeling

The key idea in CBT is that a situation does not create your feeling directly. Your **interpretation** of the situation, the thought, sits in the middle. Two women can be told "The manager wants to see you" and feel very different things, because one thinks "I am in trouble" and the other thinks "Maybe she has news."

Automatic thought appears
Feeling follows

Changing the thought in the middle changes the feeling at the end.

Thinking trap
What it sounds like

What went partly well?
Mind-reading

These traps were described by Beck and later popularised by David Burns. Everybody falls into them, especially when tired, hungry or stressed. The goal is not to never have these thoughts. The goal is to spot them faster.
The five-column thought record
**Situation:** what happened, as a camera would record it. Who, what, where, when.
**Automatic thought:** the exact words that went through your mind.
**Feeling:** name it (anxious, ashamed, angry, sad) and rate it from 0 to 100.
**Evidence:** list facts that support the thought, then facts that do not. Facts only, not feelings.
**Balanced thought:** a fairer statement that takes all the evidence into account. Then re-rate the feeling.
Worked example: a thought record after a church meeting
For example, Amaka, 31, a hairdresser in Owerri, was asked to give a short report at her women's fellowship meeting. Her voice shook and she lost her place once.
Situation: Sunday, fellowship meeting, I gave a two-minute report on the welfare fund.
Automatic thought: "Everybody saw I was shaking. I am useless at speaking." Feeling: shame, 80 out of 100.
Evidence for: my voice shook, I paused for about five seconds.
Evidence against: I gave all the figures correctly; two women thanked me; the chairlady asked me to report again next month; nobody laughed.
Balanced thought: "I was nervous and lost my place once, and I still delivered a clear, correct report. Speaking is a skill I am building."
Amaka re-rates her shame at 35 out of 100. She has not lied to herself; she has simply looked at all the facts instead of only the scary ones.
Make the balanced thought believable
Do not replace "I am useless" with "I am the best speaker in Nigeria." Your mind will reject it. Aim for a thought that is true and fair, often using "and": "I was nervous, and I did it."
Talk to yourself like a good friend

Psychologist Kristin Neff, who studies **self-compassion**, suggests a simple test: would you speak to a friend the way you speak to yourself? If your friend shook during a report, you would not call her useless. You would say, "Well done for standing up. It gets easier." Saying that to yourself is not weakness or pride. Research on self-compassion links it with more willingness to try again after mistakes.

Practise this daily for two weeks. Each evening, write one moment when the inner critic spoke, the trap it used, and the kinder, fairer sentence you chose instead. After a few days you will notice the critic's favourite lines repeating. Recognising "Ah, this is my catastrophising again" is already half of the work.
When thoughts feel too heavy

If your inner voice tells you that you are worthless, that others would be better without you, or that there is no point in living, do not handle that alone with a worksheet. Speak to a doctor, a trusted health worker or a mental health service as soon as you can. In an emergency in Nigeria, call 112.

How past experiences shape the story you tell about yourself
Identify early messages that still shape your self-belief
Distinguish facts about the past from conclusions you drew

Much of what we believe about ourselves was learned before we could question it. A teacher who mocked your reading aloud, a relative who said "girls do not need too much book", a parent who praised your brother's brains and your sister's beauty: these messages can settle into **core beliefs** such as "I am not clever" or "My voice does not matter." In CBT, core beliefs are deep, general rules about yourself, other people and the world.

Core beliefs are powerful because they act like a filter. If you believe "I am not clever", you notice every mistake and quietly ignore every success. Over years, the filter makes the belief feel more and more true, even when it is not.
A woman thinking with lines connecting past memories
Old messages can become filters that shape what we notice today.
Facts versus conclusions

The first step is to separate **what happened** from **what you concluded**. What happened is fixed. The conclusion you drew as a child or young woman can be re-examined now, with adult eyes and more information.
Fact or conclusion?
What happened (fact)
What I concluded (belief)
You cannot change the left column, but you can test the right one.
I failed maths in SS2
My aunt called me "olodo"
My first business closed
I am not intelligent
I will never amount to much
I am not a business person
Why early messages stick
They came from people with power over us, such as parents, teachers or elders.
They were repeated, and repetition makes ideas feel true.
As children we lacked the information to see other explanations, for example that a teacher was overworked or that a family had no money for lessons.
Culture can add weight: messages about how a "good woman" should behave are often shared by a whole community.
Testing an old belief with today's evidence
Write the belief in one short sentence, for example "I am not intelligent."
Write where it came from: who said or did what, and when.
List other explanations for that event. Was there missing support, poverty, illness, a bad teacher?
List evidence from your adult life that does not fit the belief. Be specific and include ordinary things.
Write an updated belief that fits all the evidence.
Worked example: "I am not intelligent"

For example, Halima, 44, from Kaduna, left school after JSS3 when her family could no longer pay fees. A teacher once told her she was "too slow for secondary school." She has believed she is not intelligent ever since.
Other explanations: she was often absent helping her mother sell; the class had over 70 pupils; she had no textbooks.
Adult evidence: she manages a provisions shop and keeps accurate records of about 60 customers who buy on credit.
She calculates profit margins in her head faster than her nephew with a calculator.
She learned to use a POS terminal and Opay in one week by watching and practising.
Updated belief: "I missed schooling because of money, not ability. I learn quickly when I have the chance, and my shop proves it."
Halima does not erase the painful memory. She changes the meaning she takes from it, and that opens the door to enrolling in an adult literacy and numeracy class.

Psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described the **impostor phenomenon** in 1978: capable, successful people who believe they are frauds and that their success is luck. It is common among women who rose further than their families expected. Knowing the name helps. When the thought "They will find out I do not belong" comes, you can recognise it as a familiar pattern, not a fact.

When the past is too painful

Some memories are not simply unhelpful messages but real harm. If thinking about the past brings flashbacks, panic, numbness or overwhelming distress, stop the exercise. That is a sign to work with a trained counsellor, psychologist or doctor, who can help you safely. You do not have to face it alone.

Reviewing your past this way is not about blaming parents or teachers. Many of them were doing their best with what they had. It is about giving yourself permission to update a story that was written before you had all the facts.

Expect the old belief to return now and then, especially on hard days. That is normal. Beliefs held for decades do not disappear after one exercise. Each time it returns, answer it with your evidence list. Over months, the updated belief becomes the one that comes to mind first.

Confidence, arrogance and humility: finding the healthy balance

Many Nigerian women are taught from childhood to be humble, to "not carry shoulder", to avoid "forming". These are good values when they mean respect for others. But sometimes humility is confused with **shrinking**: hiding skills, refusing credit, apologising for existing. Real confidence sits between two extremes: arrogance on one side and self-doubt on the other.
A balance scale
Healthy confidence balances belief in yourself with respect for others.
Three ways of carrying yourself
Arrogance versus confidence
Arrogance
Healthy confidence
Arrogance needs others to be smaller; confidence does not.

Dismisses other views
Hides mistakes or blames others
Needs constant praise
Knows strengths and limits

Owns mistakes and fixes them
Feels steady without applause

Arrogance often grows from **insecurity**. A person who must always win the argument may be afraid of being seen as weak. Healthy confidence is quieter. It can say "I do not know" or "You are right, I was wrong" without feeling destroyed, because the person's worth does not depend on winning every moment.

Low confidence also has a cost. When you hide your skills, your team, your customers and your community lose what you could contribute. A seamstress who will not show her best designs loses sales. A nurse who will not speak up about a mistake she noticed may put a patient at risk. Shrinking is not automatically the humble or safe choice.
Accurate self-assessment
The goal is to see yourself **accurately**: neither bigger nor smaller than the evidence. Researchers sometimes call this calibration. You can practise it with three questions:
What am I genuinely good at, and what evidence shows it? (sales figures, feedback, results)
What am I still learning, and what would help me improve?
What do people I trust say about my strengths and weak spots?
Saying what you did, without boasting
Shrinking
Boasting
Confident and accurate
"It was nothing, anybody could do it."
"Without me, this event would have collapsed."
"Thank you. I organised the catering for 150 guests and it went well."
"I just helped small."
"I am the best tailor in this whole town."
"I sewed all 12 uniforms and delivered two days early."
"Sorry, I am not an expert but..."
"Listen to me, I know better than all of you."
"From my five years running a shop, I would suggest..."
Notice what the confident column does. It states **facts and numbers**, it says thank you, and it does not put anybody down. It is not proud; it is honest.
Worked example: accepting a compliment and asking for feedback
For example, Funmi, 29, a junior accounts officer in Ibadan, prepared a budget that her manager praised at a staff meeting. Her habit is to say "Ah, it was nothing."
Instead, she says: "Thank you, sir. It took about three days to reconcile the figures and I am glad it is useful."
After the meeting she asks: "What is one thing I could do better on the next budget?"
Her manager suggests she add a short summary page. Funmi writes it down.
On the next budget she adds the summary and mentions it: "I added a one-page summary as you suggested."
Funmi has accepted credit, shown openness to learning and built a reputation as someone both skilled and teachable. That combination is what people usually mean by humble confidence.
The "thank you, full stop" rule
When someone praises you, say "Thank you" and stop. Do not add "but", do not list what was wrong. If you want, add one fact: "Thank you, I worked hard on it." Practise this until it feels normal.
Feedback keeps confidence honest

A confident person does not fear feedback; she uses it. Ask specific questions such as "What is one thing I did well, and one thing I could improve?" Specific questions get useful answers. Then thank the person, even if the feedback stings, and decide what to act on. Over time, this habit protects you from both arrogance and self-doubt, because your view of yourself keeps being checked against reality.
Respect and confidence can live together

In many Nigerian homes and workplaces, respect for elders and seniors is expected, and that is valuable. Confidence does not mean dropping respect. You can greet properly, use titles such as "Ma" or "Sir", wait your turn, and still state your idea clearly. For example: "Ma, with respect, may I suggest another option? Last month we tried the same supplier and the delivery came late twice." The tone is respectful; the content is clear and backed by facts.
Use respectful openings: "With respect", "If I may", "Please permit me to add".
Then speak in full sentences, without trailing off or apologising for your idea.
Support your point with a fact, a number or an example.
Accept the final decision gracefully if it goes another way, and note what you learned.

This balance is something you build over time. Watch women you admire who are both respected and respectful. Notice what they say, how long they speak and how they handle disagreement. That is vicarious learning, one of the four sources of confidence from Lesson 1.

Arrogance often hides insecurity; confidence can admit mistakes.
State achievements with facts, gratitude and no put-downs.
Accept compliments with "thank you" and ask for specific feedback.

Confidence needs solid ground. In this module you map your real strengths, set and track small goals that create mastery experiences, use your body and breathing to steady yourself, and arrange the people and habits around you so they lift you up.

Ask a group of women "What are you good at?" and many will go quiet, laugh, or say "Nothing special." Then ask what their neighbours come to them for, and the answers flow: "Everybody calls me to settle quarrels", "I am the one who plans the family events", "People bring their children to me for lessons." Strengths are often hidden in plain sight because we take them for granted.
Confidence built on vague praise is fragile. Confidence built on **known, evidenced strengths** is steady. This lesson helps you collect that evidence.

Skills and knowledge can be listed on a CV. Character strengths are harder to see but just as important. Psychologists Christopher Peterson and Martin Seligman, working with the VIA Institute on Character, described **24 character strengths** found across cultures, such as bravery, kindness, teamwork, gratitude and self-regulation. Building your strengths inventory
**List what you do often.** Go through a normal week: home, work, business, church or mosque, community. Write every task you handle.
**Mark what goes well.** Tick the tasks where things usually turn out right or people are pleased.
**Ask "what makes it go well?"** Behind "I plan family events well" might be organisation, budgeting and calm under pressure.
**Add evidence.** For each strength, write one specific example with a number, date or result.
**Ask three people.** Send a short message to three people who know you in different settings.
Worked example: Kemi's strengths inventory
For example, Kemi, 35, is a mother of three in Abeokuta who sells adire fabric from home. She believes she has "no real skills" because she did not finish university.

Weekly tasks she listed: keeping school runs on time, selling adire to about 25 regular customers, keeping a sales notebook, mediating between two quarrelling neighbours, running the women's savings group (esusu) for 12 members.
What makes them go well: reliability, colour sense, record keeping, fairness, trustworthiness with money.
Evidence: the esusu group has run for three years with no missing money; her sales notebook shows she sold about 140 pieces last year; two customers have referred their friends.
Feedback from three people (sister, customer, esusu member) all mentioned "honest" and "organised".

Kemi's statement: "I am organised, honest with money and good with colour. Twelve women trust me with their savings, and my customers send me referrals." She now uses this when she approaches a boutique to stock her fabric.

Strengths, not perfection

Knowing your strengths does not mean ignoring weaknesses. It means you start from what works. Research from the strengths-based approach in positive psychology suggests people feel more engaged when they use their top strengths regularly. Practically, this means choosing roles and businesses that use what you are good at, and getting help or training for the rest. A woman who is excellent at sales but weak at bookkeeping can learn basic records or partner with someone who enjoys numbers.

Compare: "I want to speak up more" with "I will share at least one idea at each of the four fellowship meetings in the next month." The second tells you exactly what to do and lets you count your wins.
Make the steps small enough

A useful test: rate your confidence that you can complete the step this week from 0 to 10. If it is below 7, make the step smaller. Small does not mean unimportant. A step you actually complete builds more confidence than a big step you avoid.

If-then plans

Psychologist Peter Gollwitzer studied **implementation intentions**, simple plans in the form "When situation X happens, I will do Y." Many studies found that people who make these plans are more likely to follow through than people who only set a goal. They work because the decision is made in advance, so you do not have to rely on willpower in the moment.
"When the chairlady asks for comments, I will raise my hand within the first minute."
"When I finish breakfast on Monday, I will post one product photo on my WhatsApp status."
"If I feel like skipping, then I will do just the first five minutes."
Worked example: a four-week goal for selling online

For example, Blessing, 27, bakes cakes in Port Harcourt but only sells to people who already know her. She is nervous about promoting herself. Her SMART goal: "Get three new cake orders from people outside my family through WhatsApp by 30 November."
Week 1: post one clear photo of a cake on WhatsApp status, three times this week. Confidence rating: 9.
Week 2: post photos plus a price list (for example, a 6-inch cake from about ₦15,000, marked approximate) and send it to 10 contacts who are not family.
Week 3: ask two happy customers for a short written review and share it with their permission.
Week 4: join one local buy-and-sell WhatsApp group and post an offer, following the group rules.
If-then plan: "When I put the kids to bed on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, I will post my status."
By week 4 Blessing has four new orders. More importantly, she has twelve logged actions she was once afraid of. Her confidence in self-promotion moves from 3 to 7 out of 10.

Celebrate on purpose

At the end of each week, look at your tracker and name your wins aloud or write them down. A small reward helps: a favourite drink, a walk, a call with a friend. Celebrating teaches your brain that effort leads to good things.

If you miss a step, do not throw the whole plan away. That is all-or-nothing thinking from Lesson 2. Ask: was the step too big, was the timing wrong, or did something unexpected happen? Adjust and continue. Progress counts more than a perfect record.

Pick a goal that matters to you but is not your scariest challenge. Good first goals are ones that happen often, so you get many chances to practise: speaking at a weekly meeting, posting products, asking one question in class, making one sales call a day. Rare, high-stakes events such as a job interview are better as a later goal, once you have built a habit of small wins. Share your goal with one supportive person and tell them your weekly results. Body, breath and appearance: steadying yourself physically

Bandura's fourth source of self-efficacy is your **physical and emotional state**. When your heart pounds and your hands shake, your mind often reads it as "I cannot do this." The good news is that you can influence some of these signals and change how you interpret them.
A woman sitting calmly in a meditation pose
Slow breathing and steady posture help the body stay calm under pressure.
Nerves are your body getting ready

Before a challenge, your body releases stress hormones such as adrenaline. Your heart beats faster, breathing quickens and you may feel butterflies. This is the body preparing for action, the same response that helps athletes perform. Research by psychologist Alison Wood Brooks found that people who told themselves "I am excited" before a stressful task such as public speaking tended to perform better than those who tried to tell themselves to calm down. You do not have to remove the energy; you can **label it differently**.
Slow breathing you can do anywhere

Slow, deep breathing into the belly is a widely taught way to calm the body, and the NHS recommends it in its self-help guide on breathing exercises for stress. The NHS version counts in and out for 5 each. Many people also find a slightly longer out-breath calming, as below; use whichever feels easier. You can do it in a taxi, in a corridor before an interview, or in your seat before speaking.
Sit or stand with your feet flat on the floor and your shoulders relaxed.
Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of 6, as if blowing on hot food to cool it.
For daily practice, the NHS suggests continuing for at least 5 minutes. Just before a challenge, even a shorter round of slow breaths is worth doing.
Notice your shoulders and jaw; let them soften.

Breathing and posture change the signal; reframing changes the interpretation.
Posture and presence

You may have heard of "power posing", standing like a superhero for two minutes to change your hormones. Later, larger studies did **not** confirm the hormone effects, so do not rely on that claim. However, an upright, open posture is still useful: it lets you breathe properly, project your voice and look engaged, and people around you tend to read it as attentive and capable.

Eye contact and culture

In many Nigerian settings, looking an elder directly in the eye for long can seem rude. Steady presence does not require staring. Look at the person's face naturally, glance down respectfully when culture expects it, and keep your head up and voice clear.
Appearance: comfortable, appropriate, ready

Appearance affects confidence mainly through comfort and fit for the setting. A gele that keeps slipping, shoes that pinch or an outfit you keep adjusting will take your attention away from what you came to do. You do not need expensive clothes. You need clothes that fit, are clean and suit the occasion.
Worked example: preparing for a loan interview
For example, Zainab, 40, runs a small grinding business in Kano and has a meeting at a microfinance bank about a loan of about ₦300,000 (approximate). She is nervous.
The night before, she chooses a clean, ironed outfit she has worn before and feels comfortable in, with flat shoes because she will walk from the bus stop.
She packs her documents in one folder: ID, business records for six months and her cooperative letter.
In the banking hall she does 8 slow breaths (in for 4, out for 6) while waiting.
She tells herself: "My heart is racing because this matters. I am ready."
In the meeting she sits upright, greets the officer, and places her folder on the table.
Zainab still feels nervous, but she speaks clearly and answers every question about her monthly sales. Her physical preparation freed her mind to focus on the content.

Sleep, food and water also affect confidence. A hungry, exhausted brain is more likely to fall into the thinking traps from Module 1. Before an important day, try to eat a simple meal and get as much rest as your responsibilities allow.
Your voice is part of your body

A steady voice comes from breath. When nervous, many people breathe high in the chest and speak quickly in a thin voice. Before speaking, take one slow breath into your belly, then start your first sentence a little slower than feels natural. Practise reading a short paragraph aloud each day, standing upright, aiming your voice at the far wall. Record yourself on your phone once a week and listen back. Most people are surprised that they sound calmer than they felt.

Two of Bandura's sources of confidence come from other people: **watching people like you succeed** and **encouragement from people you trust**. That means the people around you are not a side issue. They are part of the confidence system. A supportive circle will not do your work for you, but it makes the work much easier.

Mapping your circle

Think about the people you speak with in a typical week: family, friends, colleagues, customers, church or mosque members, WhatsApp groups. For each person, ask: after time with them, do I usually feel more capable or less capable?

**Close and draining:** often family or old friends. You may not cut them off, but you can limit what you share and set boundaries.
**Distant and draining:** social media accounts or groups that make you feel small. Mute, leave or limit.
Role models and mentors

A **role model** is someone you learn from by watching, even from a distance. A **mentor** is someone who knows you and gives you guidance. The most useful role models are a step or two ahead of you, in a similar situation, so their success feels possible. A woman who grew her tailoring business from one machine to four machines in your town may teach you more than a famous designer abroad.

Boundaries with discouraging people

Some people discourage you out of fear for you, jealousy or habit. A **boundary** is a clear, calm statement of what you will and will not accept. It is about your behaviour, not about controlling theirs.
Worked example: a boundary with a discouraging relative
For example, Esther, 33, in Jos, has enrolled in a computer class. Each time she mentions it, her elder cousin says, "At your age? Your mates are building houses. You are wasting money."
Esther decides to keep her goals private from her cousin for now, and to share them with her friend Ruth, who encourages her.
When the cousin raises it again, she says calmly: "I know you care about me. I have decided to do this course and I am enjoying it. Let us talk about something else."
If he continues, she repeats the same sentence once and changes the subject.
She joins a WhatsApp group of other learners from her class, where people share progress.
The cousin's comments still come sometimes, but they no longer stop Esther. After eight weeks she passes her first module test and shares the result with Ruth and her class group.
Your daily environment
Your environment includes your phone, which you may look at more than any person. Small changes help:
Mute or leave groups that constantly gossip or compare.
Follow pages that teach practical skills in your field.
Put your strengths list and goal tracker where you will see them, for example as your phone wallpaper or on the wall near your work area.
Find or start a small accountability group of three or four women who check in weekly on goals.
When home is not safe

If someone in your home controls you through threats, fear or violence, this is more than a confidence issue. Your safety comes first. Speak to someone you trust, a health worker or a recognised support organisation, and in an emergency call 112.

A supportive circle is built slowly. Start with one person who lifts you and one small change to your phone this week. Over time, the voices around you will begin to match the voice you are building inside.

Remember that support flows both ways. Encourage other women in your circle by noticing their efforts and naming them specifically: "You handled that customer complaint so calmly." Giving specific encouragement strengthens the relationship, and teaching or supporting others often reminds you of what you already know. A circle where women lift each other becomes stronger than any one member alone.

Acting Confidently

Confidence grows fastest through action. In this module you learn to act before you feel fully ready, communicate assertively instead of passively or aggressively, handle professional situations such as interviews and negotiations, and speak in public with a clear structure.
Acting before you feel ready: courage and the fear ladder
Explain why avoidance makes fear stronger over time
Build a fear ladder of graded steps for one situation

Many women wait to feel confident before they act: "When I feel ready, I will apply for that job", "When I am less shy, I will join the committee." The trouble is that the feeling rarely arrives on its own. In most cases, **courage comes first and confidence follows**. Courage is acting while fear is present. Confidence is what grows after you have done it several times.
A woman at a starting line ready to run
Courage is taking the first step before the fear has gone.
Why avoiding makes fear grow

When you avoid something you fear, you feel relief straight away. That relief teaches your brain that avoiding was the right choice, so next time the fear is a little stronger. You also miss the chance to learn that the situation was manageable. This **avoidance cycle** is well described in anxiety research, and breaking it is a core part of CBT.
The avoidance cycle
Feared situation
Anxiety rises
Avoid it
Short relief
Fear grows stronger
Avoidance brings quick relief but makes the next attempt harder.

The opposite also works. When you face a feared situation in a manageable dose and stay with it, anxiety usually rises, peaks and then falls. Each time, your brain collects new evidence: "I did it and survived." Psychologists call this gradual approach **graded exposure**.
Building a fear ladder

A fear ladder breaks one big fear into steps, from easiest to hardest. You rate each step for how anxious you expect to feel, from 0 (no anxiety) to 10 (extreme). Then you start at a step around 3 or 4 and move up only when a step feels manageable.
Name the situation you want to handle, for example speaking up in meetings.
List 6 to 10 versions of it, from very easy to very hard.
Rate each one from 0 to 10 for expected anxiety.
Put them in order, lowest to highest.
Start with a step around 3 or 4. Repeat it until your anxiety drops to about half.
Move to the next step. Keep notes after each attempt.
Worked example: Joy's fear ladder for speaking at work
For example, Joy, 26, a customer service officer at a bank branch in Abuja, never speaks in team meetings although she has good ideas.
Step 1 (anxiety 2): Say "Good morning" to everyone as the meeting starts.
Step 2 (anxiety 3): Ask one short question, for example "When is the deadline?"
Step 3 (anxiety 4): Agree with a colleague's point and add one sentence.
Step 4 (anxiety 6): Share one idea she has prepared and written down beforehand.
Step 5 (anxiety 7): Give a two-minute update on her customer complaints figures.
Step 6 (anxiety 9): Volunteer to present a small improvement proposal.
Joy spends one to two weeks on each step. By the end of two months she has done step 5 three times. Step 4, once rated 6, now feels like a 2. Her manager asks her to lead the proposal in step 6.
Predict, then test

Before each step, write down what you fear will happen and how likely you think it is. Afterwards, write what actually happened. This simple habit, used in CBT as a **behavioural experiment**, shows you how often your predictions are worse than reality.

When a task feels too big, agree with yourself to do only the first five minutes: write the first line of the application, make the first phone call, open the course website. Starting is often the hardest part. After five minutes you may continue, and if you stop, you have still taken a step. This works well alongside the if-then plans from Module 2.

Short sentences can help you act: "I can feel nervous and still do it." "Done is better than perfect." "This is step 3, not the whole ladder." Write one on a card or as your phone wallpaper.

Some fears are so strong that they cause panic attacks or stop you leaving home or doing daily tasks. Graded exposure for severe anxiety is best done with a trained therapist or psychologist. Please seek professional help if that describes you.
Remember that the aim is not to stop feeling fear. The aim is to stop fear from making your decisions. Each time you climb one rung, you show yourself that you are bigger than the fear.

Assertiveness is the ability to express your thoughts, feelings and needs **clearly and honestly, while respecting other people**. It is one of the most practical confidence skills you can learn, and it is widely taught in health, workplace and counselling settings. Being assertive does not mean being rude or "too known". It means not hiding your needs and not trampling on others.

"I" statements

An "I" statement describes your experience instead of attacking the other person. Compare "You are so careless, you always pay me late!" with "I feel stressed when payment comes late, because I need it to buy materials. Can we agree on payment by the 5th?" The first invites defence. The second invites a solution.
Formula: **"I feel [emotion] when [specific behaviour], because [effect on me]. I would like [clear request]."**
Keep the behaviour specific and observable. "When you arrive 40 minutes late" is better than "when you are disrespectful."
Make one clear request, not a list of complaints.
The DESC script for bigger conversations
The **DESC** script was developed by Sharon and Gordon Bower in their book "Asserting Yourself". It helps you plan a difficult conversation in four parts:
**D, Describe:** state the facts of the situation without blame.
**E, Express:** say how it affects you, using "I" statements.
**S, Specify:** ask for one clear, reasonable change.
**C, Consequences:** explain the positive result if the change happens (and, if needed, what you will do if it does not).
Worked example: a late-paying customer
For example, Patience, 37, a caterer in Benin City, supplied small chops for an office party worth about ₦85,000 (approximate). The client paid ₦40,000 and has delayed the balance for three weeks.
Describe: "Good afternoon, Mr Osas. I delivered the order on 12 October. ₦40,000 has been paid and ₦45,000 is outstanding."
Express: "I am concerned because I have already paid my suppliers for that order."
Specify: "Please can you pay the balance by Friday 7 November? You can transfer to my Moniepoint account."
Consequences: "That way I can keep my prices steady for your next event. If it is difficult to pay all at once, let us agree on two dates today."
Mr Osas apologises and pays ₦25,000 that week and the rest the next. Patience also decides that for future orders over ₦50,000 she will ask for 70 percent upfront, stated clearly on her invoice.
Saying no and the broken record

Many women find "no" the hardest word. A useful method is the **broken record**: calmly repeat your main message, without new excuses, until it is heard. You can show understanding, but you do not have to argue.
Request: "Please lend me ₦50,000 till month end."
You: "I understand things are tight. I am not able to lend money this month."
Request again: "Just this once, you know I will pay."
You: "I hear you. I am not able to lend money this month."
Offer an alternative if you genuinely want to: "I can help you look at the cooperative loan option."
Safety comes first

Assertiveness is a skill for respectful relationships. If speaking up could put you at risk of violence, your safety is the priority. Plan carefully, involve trusted people, and contact a support organisation or call 112 in an emergency.

Practise with low-stakes situations first: asking a trader to repackage an item, telling a friend you prefer a different meeting time, returning a wrong order. Each small assertive moment is a mastery experience that prepares you for bigger ones.
Body language that matches your words

Assertive words lose power if your body says something else. Keep your voice calm and even, at normal volume. Face the person, keep your hands relaxed, and avoid smiling nervously while making a serious request, because it can confuse the message. Listen fully when the other person replies, and show you heard them: "So you are saying the transfer delay is from your bank side." Listening is part of assertiveness, because it shows that their needs matter too. If emotions rise, it is fine to say, "Let us continue this tomorrow," and come back calmer.
Assertive communication respects both your needs and others'.

Professional situations test confidence because something real is at stake: a job, a contract, a price. The good news is that confidence at work is mostly **preparation made visible**. When you have done the homework, you have something solid to stand on.
A woman in a job interview across a desk
Preparation turns interview nerves into clear, confident answers.
Interviews: the STAR method

Many interviewers ask behavioural questions such as "Tell me about a time you solved a problem." The **STAR** method, widely recommended by career services, helps you answer clearly in about one to two minutes:

Situation
Task
Action
Result
A STAR answer tells a short, complete story with a clear result.
Part
What to say
Example sentence
Set the scene briefly
"At the pharmacy where I worked, stock records often did not match the shelves."

"I was asked to fix the stock count before the audit."

Prepare four or five STAR stories from your work, business, volunteering or community life. One story can often answer several questions. Women returning to work after raising children can use stories from running a home budget, organising events, or leading a church or community group. These are real experiences.
Meetings: prepare, speak early, follow up
**Prepare:** read the agenda and write one point or question you want to raise.
**Speak early:** contribute within the first ten minutes. The longer you wait, the harder it feels.
**Be brief and clear:** state your point in two or three sentences, with one fact or example.
**Claim your idea:** if someone repeats your idea later, say calmly, "Yes, building on what I suggested earlier..."
**Follow up:** send a short message or email after the meeting summarising your point or action.
Negotiating prices and pay

Many women undercharge for their products or accept the first salary offer because asking for more feels greedy. A fair price is not greed. It covers your costs, your time and a reasonable profit. Confidence in negotiation comes from **research** and from knowing your **walk-away point**, the lowest you will accept.
Research what similar products, services or roles pay in your area: ask in trade groups, check job adverts and compare prices from three or more sellers.
Calculate your costs (materials, transport, data, time) before naming a price.
Decide three numbers: your ideal price, a realistic target, and your walk-away point.
State your price once, clearly, and then pause. Do not rush to fill the silence or apologise.
If you lower the price, ask for something in return, such as a larger order or upfront payment.
Worked example: pricing a bulk order of aso-ebi
For example, Rukayat, 32, a tailor in Ilorin, is asked to sew 20 aso-ebi outfits for a wedding. The family asks her "best price". All figures are illustrative and approximate.
Her costs per outfit (fabric supplied by client): thread, lining and accessories about ₦2,500; transport and electricity share about ₦1,000. Total cost about ₦3,500.
She needs about 4 hours per outfit and wants at least ₦1,500 per hour for her labour: ₦6,000.
Cost plus labour gives about ₦9,500. Other tailors nearby charge ₦12,000 to ₦15,000 for similar styles.
Her three numbers: ideal ₦14,000, target ₦12,500, walk-away ₦10,000.
She says: "For 20 outfits in this style, my price is ₦14,000 each, ready in three weeks." Then she waits.
The family offers ₦11,000. She replies: "I can do ₦12,500 if you pay 60 percent upfront and confirm all measurements by Saturday."
They agree at ₦12,500 with 60 percent upfront. Rukayat earns about ₦180,000 above her costs for the job and avoids the common mistake of pricing below cost to please the client.
A "no" is information, not rejection

If the other side refuses, ask: "What would make this work for you?" Their answer may open a new option. If the offer falls below your walk-away point, thank them politely and leave the door open. Walking away from a bad deal is a confident decision.
Watch out for job and payment scams

Be cautious of job offers that ask you to pay a "processing fee", jobs abroad that seem too good to be true, or buyers who send fake transfer alerts. Confirm payments in your actual bank or Opay or Moniepoint app before releasing goods, and never share your BVN, PIN or OTP.

Each interview, meeting or negotiation you prepare for adds to your evidence, whatever the result. Keep a simple log: what you prepared, what you said, what happened and what you learned. Over a few months, that log will show steady growth.
Workplace confidence comes mostly from visible preparation.

Speaking in front of others is one of the most common fears. The good news is that public speaking is a **skill with clear techniques**, not a gift that only some people have. Whether you are giving a report at a cooperative meeting, a vote of thanks at a wedding, a product pitch, or a talk in church, the same basics apply.
A woman speaking confidently to an audience
Clear structure and practice make speaking in public manageable.
Start with one main idea

Chris Anderson, the head of TED, argues that a good talk carries **one main idea** that the audience can take away. Many nervous speakers try to say everything. Instead, decide the single sentence you want people to remember, then choose only the points that support it.

Point 2: records. Every deposit is recorded, so there are no quarrels about who paid what.
Point 3: loans. A savings history can help the cooperative apply for a microfinance loan.

Pause after important points. A pause feels long to you but natural to the audience.

Confidence also means letting people know what you do. Visibility can be a short introduction at a meeting, a WhatsApp status about your business, a LinkedIn profile, or volunteering to lead a small project. Start with one channel you already use.

Share your work, not your private life. Avoid posting your home address, children's school details, travel plans or financial information publicly. Use the privacy settings on WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, and be cautious of strangers who move quickly from business talk to personal requests or money.

Every talk you give, however small, is a mastery experience. Keep a speaking log with the date, the audience, how long you spoke and one thing that went well. After ten entries, read the log from the beginning. The difference will be your proof.

If someone is rude or tries to argue, stay calm, thank them for the point, and offer to discuss after the meeting. Your calm response often earns more respect than a clever reply.

Sustaining Confidence

Confidence is not a finish line; it needs maintenance. In this module you learn to recover from setbacks with a growth mindset, handle comparison and envy, navigate cultural expectations about women with wisdom, and pass healthy confidence on to children and your community.
Recovering from setbacks with a growth mindset
Contrast fixed and growth mindset responses to failure
Use the word "yet" and effort-focused self-talk
Run a simple after-action review on a setback
Plan a next step within 48 hours of a disappointment

Every woman who tries new things will face setbacks: a rejected application, a failed business idea, a talk that went badly, a customer who complains loudly. Setbacks are not proof that you lack ability. They are part of the learning process. What matters most for long-term confidence is **how you interpret and respond** to them.
A small green seedling growing
Abilities grow with effort and good strategies, like a seedling with care.
Fixed and growth mindsets

Stanford psychologist **Carol Dweck** describes two broad beliefs about ability. With a **fixed mindset**, people believe ability is set: you either have it or you do not, so failure feels like a verdict on who you are. With a **growth mindset**, people believe abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others, so failure is information about what to change. Most people hold a mix of both, and the mix can change.
Two ways to read a setback
Fixed mindset
Growth mindset
The same setback can lead to giving up or to learning, depending on the belief behind it.
"I am not good at this."
Avoids the next challenge
Hides the mistake
Feels threatened by others' success
"I am not good at this yet."
Tries a new strategy
Asks what went wrong
Learns from others' success

A growth mindset is not about pretending effort alone guarantees success. Dweck has warned against this misunderstanding. Effort must be paired with **better strategies** and **asking for help**. Trying harder at the wrong method is not growth.
The first 48 hours

Right after a setback, emotions are strong. It is normal to feel disappointed, embarrassed or angry. Allow the feeling for a while without making big decisions. Then, within about two days, take one small action so the setback does not turn into avoidance.
**Feel it:** name the emotion and allow it. Talk to one supportive person.
**Check the thoughts:** watch for labelling ("I am a failure") and catastrophising ("I will never get a job"). Use your thought record from Module 1.
**Review:** do a short after-action review (below).
**Act:** choose one small next step and do it within 48 hours.
The after-action review

The after-action review is a short structured debrief originally developed by the US Army and now used by many organisations. It works just as well for personal setbacks. Answer four questions in writing:
Question
What to write
What did I plan or expect?
Your goal and what you thought would happen
What actually happened?
The facts, without blame
Why was there a difference?
Causes you can see: preparation, timing, strategy, things outside your control
What will I keep and change next time?
One thing that worked, one thing to do differently
Worked example: a failed market stall
For example, Aisha, 34, in Lagos, rented a stall at a weekend craft fair for about ₦20,000 (approximate) to sell beaded jewellery. She sold only four pieces and felt like a failure.
Expected: to sell about 30 pieces and make back her costs with profit.
Actually happened: four sales; many people stopped, looked and asked prices, then walked on.
Why: her prices were not displayed so people had to ask; she had no small, cheap items; she did not accept transfers at first and many buyers had no cash.
Keep: her colourful display attracted many visitors. Change: display clear price tags, add items under about ₦3,000, show a transfer account and QR code.
Next step within 48 hours: she messages the eight visitors who took her card, offering a 10 percent discount for orders that week.
Three of the visitors order. At the next fair, with prices displayed and transfer details on a sign, Aisha sells 22 pieces. The "failure" became the lesson that made the second fair work.
Keep a "learning file"
Alongside your wins, keep a page of setbacks and what each taught you. Over time it becomes powerful evidence that you can survive and grow from difficulty, which is itself a source of confidence.
When a setback becomes too heavy

If, after a loss or failure, you feel hopeless for weeks, cannot sleep or eat, or have thoughts of harming yourself, please speak to a doctor or mental health professional quickly. In an emergency in Nigeria, call 112. You deserve support.

Many successful people speak openly about rejections that came before their breakthroughs. You do not need famous examples, though. Look at your own life: what difficulty have you already come through? That history is your strongest proof that you can recover again.
Separate the event from your identity

Notice the difference between "I failed at this attempt" and "I am a failure." The first describes an event; the second labels your whole self. Keep your language about events: "The fair did not go well," "My application was not successful this time." This small shift keeps your self-worth steady while you work on the problem. It also makes the next step easier to see, because events can be changed and labels cannot.

"Her business is growing faster than mine." "She has a car already and we finished school the same year." "Look at her house on Instagram." Comparing ourselves with others is completely natural. Psychologist **Leon Festinger** proposed in 1954, in his social comparison theory, that people evaluate their abilities and opinions by comparing themselves with others, especially when there is no clear standard. The problem is not comparison itself but **how and with whom** we compare.

Social media shows other people's highlights, not their full story.

Can harm when

Upward comparison can inspire you, like the vicarious learning in Module 1, if the person is similar to you and you can see the steps she took. It harms when the comparison is unfair: your everyday struggles against someone else's best moments.
The highlight reel problem

Social media shows people's **highlight reels**: the wedding, the new shop opening, the holiday, the perfect outfit. It rarely shows the loans, the arguments, the failed attempts or the borrowed car. Filters and editing apps can also change how people look. When you compare your behind-the-scenes life with their highlights, you will almost always feel behind.
Before you compare, ask
Am I seeing the whole story?
Is she in a similar situation?
Can I learn her steps?
Does this help my goals?
If the answer to most is no, the comparison is not useful.
Envy as information

Envy is an uncomfortable feeling, and many of us feel ashamed of it. Instead of hiding it, use it. Envy often points to something **you want for yourself**. If you feel envy when a friend opens a salon, ask: do I want my own business? More independence? More recognition? Once you know, you can set a goal. If you feel nothing when someone buys an expensive car but strong envy when someone publishes a book, that tells you something about what matters to you.
Notice the envy without judging yourself.
Ask: what exactly does she have that I want?
Ask: is it the thing itself, or what it represents (security, respect, freedom)?

For example, Grace, 30, a teacher in Uyo, feels a sharp pang every time a former classmate posts about her growing online fashion business.
She notices the envy and writes it down instead of scrolling past with a bitter feeling.
She asks herself what she wants: not fashion, but extra income and the pride of running something of her own.
She sets a goal: start weekend lesson classes for four primary pupils by January, using her teaching strengths.
She messages her classmate: "Congratulations on your business growth. How did you get your first ten customers?"
The classmate shares tips about WhatsApp status and asking for referrals, which Grace adapts.
By February Grace has six pupils. The envy has turned into a goal that fits her own strengths, and a friendship has been strengthened instead of strained.

Remember too that someone may be comparing themselves with you right now and feeling behind. Everyone has a different starting point, different support and different responsibilities. Your path is yours.
Gratitude without denial

Noticing what is going well in your own life can soften the pull of comparison. Some people write down three good things at the end of each day: a sale made, a child's laugh, a kind word from a friend. This is not pretending problems do not exist. It is training your attention to see the full picture, including the good, instead of only what others seem to have.

Confidence does not grow in empty space. It grows inside families, communities, faiths and traditions. Nigeria has hundreds of ethnic groups and many ways of life, so there is no single "Nigerian culture". But many women share common experiences: strong respect for elders, expectations about marriage and motherhood, extended family involvement, and deep faith. These can **support** confidence or, at times, **limit** it.
A group of women standing together and celebrating
Culture and community can be a source of strength as well as expectation.
Messages that lift and messages that limit
Often supports confidence
Can limit confidence if taken to extremes
Strong community and family networks that help in hard times
"A woman should not speak when men are talking."
Long traditions of women traders and market leaders
"Your success should not be bigger than your husband's."
Faith that teaches each person has value and purpose
"What will people say?" used to stop every new idea
Respect, hospitality and care for others
Putting everyone else first until there is nothing left for yourself

Many Nigerian communities have a long history of women as traders, organisers and leaders. Market women's associations have been an important part of community life in many towns for generations. You come from people who have shown strength and resourcefulness. That is part of your heritage too.
Respect and voice together

You do not have to choose between respect and confidence. The skills from Module 3 can be adapted to cultural expectations. The key ideas are **timing, tone and channel**: choosing the right moment, using respectful words, and picking the right person or setting.
Speaking up wisely
Clarify your goal
Choose time and place
Open with respect
State point clearly
Accept, adjust, follow up
Wise timing and respectful tone help a clear message be heard.
**Timing:** a private conversation with an elder may work better than challenging them in front of everyone.
**Tone:** respectful greetings and titles show you are not dismissing tradition.
**Channel:** sometimes a trusted intermediary, such as an aunt, a pastor or imam, or the women's leader, can carry a message better.
**Facts:** support your request with practical reasons, such as costs, health, children's education or business results.
Worked example: proposing a business idea in an extended family
For example, Oluchi, 36, in Aba, wants to use part of a family-owned shop space to start a small shoe business. Decisions about the shop are made by her husband's elder brothers.
She first discusses the idea privately with her husband and agrees on the plan together.
She prepares facts: estimated start-up cost of about ₦250,000 (approximate), expected monthly rent saved, and how profits will help with the children's school fees.
She asks her husband to arrange a family meeting at a good time, after a meal, not during a busy festival.
At the meeting she greets the elders respectfully and says: "With your permission, I would like to share an idea that can help our family income."
She explains in three short points, listens to their concerns about space, and offers to use only the front corner for a six-month trial.
The elders agree to a three-month trial. Oluchi records her sales carefully and reports back. At the end of the trial they extend it. She achieved her goal while honouring the family structure.
Faith as a source of strength

For many women, faith is central. Many Christian and Muslim teachings describe each person as created with worth and purpose, and many religious communities encourage people to use their gifts. If faith matters to you, it can be a deep source of confidence: prayer or reflection before a challenge, scriptures that remind you of your worth, and faith communities that offer support and mentoring. Some women find that their faith leaders are strong supporters of their education and business growth.
Respect your own values

This lesson does not ask you to reject tradition or faith. It asks you to notice which messages help you live well and which hold you back unfairly. You decide, in line with your values, which changes to pursue and at what pace.
Navigating "What will people say?"

Concern for reputation is real, especially in close communities. When "what will people say?" comes up, ask two questions: Is this action right and good according to my values? And who exactly are "the people", and do their opinions affect my real life? Often the imagined judgement is much worse than reality, which is the mind-reading trap from Module 1.
Harmful practices and abuse

Culture should never be used to justify violence, forced marriage, denying medical care or other harm. If you or someone you know faces this, contact a trusted health worker, a recognised women's rights organisation or the police. In an emergency, call 112.

Confident women do not stop being Nigerian, Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, Tiv, Efik or any other identity. They carry their culture with pride while helping it grow. Every woman who speaks up wisely makes it a little easier for the next woman.

The confidence you build does not stop with you. Children watch how you speak to yourself, how you handle mistakes and how you treat others. Women around you watch too. This final lesson helps you pass on healthy confidence to the next generation and your community.

Children learn confidence by watching and by being trusted with small tasks.

In a well-known 1998 study, Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck found that children praised for being "smart" after a task were more likely to avoid harder challenges and to lose motivation after failure than children praised for their effort. The lesson for parents: **praise the process**, meaning the effort, strategies, persistence and improvement, rather than fixed traits like "clever" or "beautiful".

Children build self-efficacy the same way adults do: through **mastery experiences**. Giving them real, age-appropriate tasks lets them collect evidence that they are capable. Offering simple choices also helps them practise decision-making.

**Older children:** sweep a room, buy small items at the shop with correct change, help a younger sibling with reading.
**Teenagers:** plan a family meal and its budget, manage their own pocket money, help in the family business with real responsibility.
Safety with responsibility

Match tasks to the child's age and ability. Supervise anything involving fire, sharp knives, electricity, roads or handling money in busy places. Teach children about online safety, and that no adult should ask them to keep secrets about touching or gifts.
Raising confident girls and boys

Girls often receive messages to be quiet, pleasing and small. Boys often receive messages that they must never show fear or sadness. Both limit confidence. Encourage girls to give opinions, take part in sports or debate, and lead group tasks. Encourage boys to name feelings and to respect girls' voices. Worked example: a growth-minded response to a poor result
For example, Bimpe, 39, in Ibadan, sees that her 11-year-old daughter Tolu scored 9 out of 30 in a maths test. Tolu says, "I am just not a maths person."
Bimpe stays calm and says: "I can see you are disappointed. Let us look at it together."
They look at the mistakes: most are in fractions. Bimpe says, "So it is not all of maths. It is fractions, and fractions can be learned. You have not mastered them yet."
They agree a plan: 15 minutes of fraction practice four evenings a week, using her textbook and free videos on Khan Academy when data allows.
Bimpe praises effort each evening: "You stuck with that hard one for five minutes."
Three weeks later, Tolu scores 18 out of 30 on a class test.
Bimpe praises the improvement and the practice: "Your work on fractions paid off." Tolu learns that ability grows with effort and strategy, a lesson more valuable than any single score.

Mastery experiences
Physical states
Watching celebrities
Doing a task yourself and succeeding provides the most convincing evidence of ability.

What others might think
A positive affirmation

"I am the best in this company."

What confidence is
Four sources of I can do this
Mastery: doing it yourself and succeeding
Watching someone like you succeed
Confidence is not feeling no fear. Psychologists call it self-efficacy: your belief that you can handle a particular task.
It is about a task, not your whole self. You can be sure of yourself cooking for fifty guests, and unsure about speaking at a PTA meeting.
The strongest source is mastery: doing the task yourself and succeeding, even in small steps. Like selling your first ten bottles of zobo and getting paid.
Next is watching someone like you succeed. Your neighbour who started with the same capital convinces you more than a celebrity.
Then encouragement from people you trust.
And how you read your body. A racing heart before a meeting can mean fear, or it can mean your body is getting ready.
Worked example
Ngozi rates her confidence task by task
Weighing and pricing rice: 9 out of 10
WhatsApp price list to 30 customers: 4
Asking her cooperative for a loan: 3
Starts with WhatsApp: watch once, then do
Five orders later, she re-rates it at 7
Action usually comes first. The feeling follows the evidence.
For example, Ngozi is 38 and sells foodstuff in Enugu. She rates her confidence from 0 to 10 for three tasks. Weighing and pricing rice: 9, because she has done it daily for twelve years.
Sending a price list on WhatsApp to 30 customers: only 4.
Asking her cooperative for a loan: 3. She has never spoken at a meeting.
She starts with the lowest-risk task. Her niece shows her once, then she does it herself.
She gets five orders, and re-rates WhatsApp at 7. Confidence can grow at 25, 45 or 65. Do not wait to feel confident before you start.
Catch, check, change
Amaka's thought record
Situation: a two-minute report at fellowship
Thought: I am useless at speaking
Feeling: shame, 80 out of 100
Evidence: figures correct, two women thanked her
Balanced thought, then shame drops to 35
A balanced thought is fair and believable, not falsely positive.
Most of us carry a harsh inner critic. You cannot switch it off, but you can question it.
For example, Amaka, a hairdresser in Owerri, gave a short report at her women's fellowship. Her voice shook and she lost her place once.
Her automatic thought: everybody saw I was shaking. I am useless at speaking. That trap is called labelling.
She names the feeling, shame, and rates it 80 out of 100.
Now the facts. Her voice shook. But she gave all the figures correctly, two women thanked her, and the chairlady asked her to report again next month.
Her balanced thought: I was nervous and lost my place once, and I still delivered a clear, correct report. Her shame drops to 35.
Do not swap I am useless for I am the best speaker in Nigeria. Your mind will reject it. Use and: I was nervous, and I did it.
Old stories
What happened, or what I concluded?
My aunt called me olodo
What I concluded
Many beliefs about ourselves were learned before we could question them. What happened is fixed.
But the conclusion you drew can be tested now. For example, Halima left school after JSS3 because her family could not pay fees, and a teacher called her too slow.
Today she keeps accurate records for about 60 credit customers and learned a POS terminal in one week. Her updated belief: I missed school because of money, not ability.
Humble confidence
Say what you did, without boasting
It was nothing, anybody could do it.
Without me, this event would have collapsed.
Thank you. I organised the catering for 150 guests and it went well.
Being humble is good. But hiding your skills is shrinking, and your customers and community lose what you could give.
Arrogance goes the other way. It needs other people to be smaller.
Healthy confidence states facts, says thank you, and puts nobody down.
When someone praises you, say thank you, full stop. For example, Funmi used to say, it was nothing. Now she says thank you, and asks her manager what she could do better next time.
Key points
Remember
Confidence is belief you can handle a task
Small tasks done yourself are the strongest source
Check thoughts against facts
Separate what happened from what you concluded
Thank you, full stop, then ask for feedback
To remember. Confidence grows task by task, from small actions. Check your thoughts against facts. Test old beliefs with today's evidence. And accept praise with thank you.
This course is not therapy. If your inner voice says there is no point in living, do not handle it alone. Speak to a doctor or health worker as soon as you can. In an emergency in Nigeria, call 112.

Small wins
Blessing's four-week ladder
Week 1: post one cake photo, three times
Week 2: send a price list to 10 contacts
Week 3: share two customer reviews
Week 4: post in one buy-and-sell group
Doing things yourself and succeeding is the strongest source of confidence. Small wins create that on purpose.

For example, Blessing bakes cakes in Port Harcourt but is nervous about promoting herself. Her SMART goal: three new orders from people outside her family, through WhatsApp, by 30 November. Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Week one is tiny: post one cake photo on her status, three times. Her confidence rating for it is 9.
Each week is a little bigger. Rate every step from 0 to 10. Below 7? Make it smaller.
She also makes an if-then plan. When I put the kids to bed on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, I will post my status.
By week 4 she has four new orders, and her confidence in self-promotion moves from 3 to 7.
Steady your body
Slow breathing before a challenge
Feet flat, shoulders relaxed
Breathe in through your nose for 4
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6
Practise daily for at least 5 minutes
Soften your shoulders and jaw
Nerves are your body getting ready. Tell yourself: I am ready.
A racing heart before a challenge is your body preparing for action. You do not have to remove that energy. You can label it differently.
For example, Zainab runs a grinding business in Kano and has a loan meeting at a microfinance bank.
In the banking hall she sits with her feet flat and shoulders relaxed.
She breathes in through her nose for 4, and out slowly through her mouth for 6, like blowing on hot food. She does 8 slow breaths. For daily practice, keep going for at least 5 minutes.
Then she tells herself, my heart is racing because this matters. I am ready. She still feels nervous, but she answers every question clearly.
Shrinking or steady?
Closed, shrinking
Shoulders rounded, arms folded
The smallest corner seat
Open, steady
Shoulders back and relaxed
Eyes on the speaker's face
Calm pace, heard at the back
Sitting where you can be seen
A shrinking posture squeezes your breath and your voice.

An upright, open posture lets you breathe, project your voice and look engaged. Steady presence does not mean staring. Where culture expects it, glance down respectfully, and keep your head up and voice clear.
Wear clean clothes that fit and suit the occasion. A slipping gele or pinching shoes steal your attention.
Your circle
Map who lifts you and who drains you
Close and lifting: share goals and wins
Distant and lifting: move them closer
Close and draining: share less, set limits
Distant and draining: mute or leave
After time with someone, do you usually feel more capable, or less?
Share your goals with close people who lift you. Move helpful mentors and role models closer. The best role model is a woman a step or two ahead of you, in your own town.

Key points
Remember
Back every strength with real evidence
Small SMART steps you rate 7 or more
Breathe in for 4, out for 6
Upright posture, clothes that fit
Spend time with people who lift you
To remember. Back your strengths with evidence. Take small steps you can finish. Breathe slowly and stand tall. And build a circle that lifts you.

The fear ladder
Joy climbs one step at a time
Step 1: say good morning to everyone
Step 2: ask one short question
Step 4: share one prepared idea
Step 5: give a two-minute update
Step 6: present a small proposal
Courage comes first. Confidence grows after you act.
When you avoid something you fear, you feel relief. But that relief makes the fear stronger next time.
For example, Joy works at a bank branch in Abuja and never speaks in team meetings. She builds a fear ladder, rating each step from 0 to 10 for anxiety.
Step one, rated 2: say good morning as the meeting starts. Step two, rated 3: ask one short question.
Later steps: share one idea she has written down beforehand, then give a two-minute update on her figures. She spends one to two weeks on each step.
Step four, once rated 6, now feels like a 2. Her manager asks her to lead the proposal.
Before each step, write what you fear will happen. Afterwards, write what really happened. Usually reality is kinder.
Assertive communication
Passive or assertive?
It is okay, no problem
I need it by Friday
Passive speech says, your needs matter and mine do not. It leads to resentment.
Assertive speech says, my needs and yours both matter. It is clear and respectful.
Use an I statement. I feel stressed when payment comes late, because I need it to buy materials. Can we agree on payment by the 5th?
Worked example
DESC: Patience asks for her balance
Describe: 40,000 paid, 45,000 outstanding
Express: I have already paid my suppliers
Specify: please pay the balance by Friday
Consequences: steady prices, or two dates
For example, Patience, a caterer in Benin City, supplied small chops worth about 85,000 naira. The client has delayed the balance for three weeks. She plans the call with DESC.
Describe the facts without blame. I delivered on 12 October. 40,000 naira has been paid and 45,000 is outstanding.
Express how it affects you. I am concerned because I have already paid my suppliers.
Specify one clear change. Please can you pay the balance by Friday?
Consequences. That way I can keep my prices steady. If it is difficult, let us agree on two dates today.
He pays within two weeks. To say no, calmly repeat your main message without new excuses. I am not able to lend money this month.
Know your costs
Rukayat prices one aso-ebi outfit
For example, Rukayat, a tailor in Ilorin, is asked for her best price on 20 aso-ebi outfits.
Thread, lining, accessories
Transport and electricity share
Her labour: 4 hours
Naira figures are approximate.
Many women undercharge because asking for more feels greedy. A fair price covers your costs, your time and a reasonable profit.
For example, Rukayat is asked to sew 20 aso-ebi outfits. The client supplies the fabric.
Thread, lining and accessories cost about 2,500 naira per outfit. Transport and electricity add about 1,000.
Each outfit takes about 4 hours, and she values her labour at 1,500 naira an hour. That is 6,000.
So cost plus labour is about 9,500 naira per outfit. Other tailors nearby charge 12,000 to 15,000 naira.
Negotiating
Three numbers, then pause
Ideal price: 14,000
Realistic target: 12,500
Walk-away point: 10,000
Say it once, clearly, then wait
Lower only for something in return
Never price below cost. Confirm payment in your app first.
Before she speaks, she decides three numbers. Ideal, 14,000. Target, 12,500. Walk-away point, 10,000.
She says, for 20 outfits in this style, my price is 14,000 naira each, ready in three weeks. Then she waits.
The family offers 11,000. She replies, I can do 12,500 if you pay 60 percent upfront and confirm measurements by Saturday. They agree.
Never price below cost to please a client. And watch for fake transfer alerts. Confirm payment in your actual bank app before releasing goods, and never share your BVN, PIN or OTP.
Public speaking
Greet, then a short story, question or fact. About 30 seconds.
Each point with an example. About 2 minutes.
Repeat the main idea and say what you want people to do.
Build every talk around one main idea. For example, Chinwe, a cooperative treasurer in Onitsha, wants members to save in a group bank account.
She opens with a hook. Last year, two of our members lost their savings to fire and theft.
Then three points: safety, records, and loans.
She closes: let us vote today to open a group account.

Remember
Climb a fear ladder, one step at a time
I feel, when, because, I would like
DESC: describe, express, specify, consequences
Know cost, target and walk-away price
One main idea, practised aloud
To remember. Act before you feel ready, one step at a time. Speak with I statements and plan hard talks with DESC. Know your numbers before you negotiate. And build each talk around one idea.
